questions.title: Carbon dioxide crosses the membrane by simple diffusion
questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: SCU-FBS102 > Physiology > Cell Physiology > Membrane Transport
questions.question: Which of the following molecules can most easily cross the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane by simple diffusion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glucose is a relatively large, polar molecule that cannot cross the hydrophobic lipid bilayer directly; it requires specific facilitated-diffusion carrier proteins such as GLUT transporters.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Amino acids are polar and often charged at physiological pH, so they cannot diffuse directly through the lipid bilayer and instead require dedicated membrane transporters.
explanations.C: Correct. Carbon dioxide is a small, nonpolar, uncharged gas that dissolves readily in the hydrophobic interior of the lipid bilayer, allowing it to diffuse directly across the membrane down its partial-pressure gradient with no transporter needed. Polar or charged solutes such as glucose and amino acids, by contrast, cannot cross the bilayer unassisted and require a specific membrane transporter.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Large plasma proteins are far too big and hydrophilic to cross the lipid bilayer by simple diffusion under any circumstance; their movement across membranes, when it occurs, requires vesicular transport.

questions.learning_objective: State that carbon dioxide crosses the plasma membrane by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer because it is small, nonpolar and lipid soluble.
